rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: The most stable oxidation state of Iron is :
rows.solution:
The most stable oxidation state of iron is \(+3\).

Iron is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^6 4s^2\). Losing the two \(4s\) electrons gives \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\), which is \(3d^6\); losing one more gives \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\), which is \(3d^5\) — an exactly HALF-FILLED subshell, with five parallel electrons and the extra exchange stability that brings.

So the third electron comes away unusually easily, and the ion it leaves behind is unusually settled. Iron(II) in solution is oxidised by air to iron(III) for exactly this reason, and the potential \(E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}}\) is accordingly small and positive.

The \(+4\) state is not reached in ordinary chemistry, and no metal shows a \(-2\) state.

rows.subtopic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
rows.stem: The product formed as a result of reaction of \(\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) followed by hydrolysis is :
rows.solution:
The product is ETHANOIC ACID, \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\).

The carbon of a Grignard reagent carries a large partial NEGATIVE charge, so it attacks the electron-poor carbon of carbon dioxide. The addition gives the magnesium salt of the acid, and hydrolysis then frees it:
\(\mathrm{CH_3MgBr} + \mathrm{CO_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3COOMgBr} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

Note what the carbon count does: carbon dioxide adds ONE carbon to the reagent's skeleton, so a one-carbon Grignard gives a two-carbon acid. This is the standard way of lengthening a chain by one and putting a carboxyl group on the end.

Methanoic acid would require a Grignard reagent with no carbon at all; the aldehyde and the ketone would need a different carbonyl partner entirely.

options.label: B
options.text: nitrogenous base, pentose sugar and phosphoric acid

rows.solution:
A nucleotide is composed of a NITROGENOUS BASE, A PENTOSE SUGAR AND PHOSPHORIC ACID — all three.

The parts join in a fixed order. The base attaches to \(\mathrm{C_1}\) of the sugar, and that two-part unit is called a NUCLEOSIDE. The phosphate then esterifies the hydroxyl at \(\mathrm{C_5}\), and the three-part unit is the NUCLEOTIDE.

The distinction between the two names is what the other options are testing. A nucleoside has two components; a nucleotide has three. It is the phosphate that makes the difference, and it is the phosphate that links one sugar to the next to build the backbone of the strand.

rows.stem: Which of the following alkyl halides will undergo \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction most readily ?
rows.solution:
Among a set of tertiary halides differing only in the halogen, the IODIDE reacts fastest by the unimolecular route.

With the same carbon skeleton in every case, the only variable is how good a leaving group the halogen makes. The slow step of an \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction is the carbon-halogen bond breaking to give the carbocation, so the WEAKER that bond, the faster the reaction.

Bond strength falls steadily down the group as the halogen grows larger and its orbital overlaps carbon's less well: \(\mathrm{C-F}\) is much the strongest, then \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\), \(\mathrm{C-Br}\), and \(\mathrm{C-I}\) the weakest. The iodide ion is also the most stable of the four anions, being the largest and best able to spread its charge.

So the order runs iodide, bromide, chloride, fluoride — and the fluoride is so unreactive that it is hardly used for substitution at all.

A note on the printing. The four options are written \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3 - X}\), with the central carbon MISSING; they should read \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C - X}\), the tert-butyl halides. The marking scheme records the error and instructs examiners to award the mark to any attempt. The chemistry above is what the question intended to test, and it does not depend on the missing atom.

rows.stem: Phenol dimerises in benzene having van't Hoff factor \(0{\cdot}54\). Its degree of association is :
rows.solution:
Phenol dimerises, so the number of particles FALLS and the van't Hoff factor comes out below 1 — as it has, at \(0{\cdot}54\).

For ASSOCIATION into \(n\) molecules the degree is
\(\alpha = \dfrac{1 - i}{1 - \frac{1}{n}}\)

A dimer means two molecules combine into one, so \(n = 2\) and the denominator is \(1 - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\):
\(\alpha = \dfrac{1 - 0{\cdot}54}{0{\cdot}5} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}46}{0{\cdot}5}\)

\(\alpha = 0{\cdot}92\)

So 92% of the phenol is present as dimers — which is why the observed particle count is barely half the formula count.

The trap is \(0{\cdot}46\), the numerator left undivided. Dividing by \(\frac{1}{2}\) DOUBLES it, and forgetting that step is the commonest error here.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
A reaction \(\mathrm{A_2} + \mathrm{B_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{AB}\) occurs by the following mechanism :
\(\mathrm{A_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{A} + \mathrm{A}\) (slow)
\(\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{AB} + \mathrm{B}\) (fast)
\(\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{AB}\) (fast)
Its order would be :
rows.solution:
The order is ONE.

For a multi-step reaction the rate is set by the SLOWEST step, because everything after it waits on it. The slow step here is
\(\mathrm{A_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{A} + \mathrm{A}\)
which involves ONE molecule of \(\mathrm{A_2}\) and nothing else, so
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A_2}]\)
and the reaction is first order overall.

\(\mathrm{B_2}\) does not appear in the rate law at all, even though it is a reactant in the balanced equation — it enters only in a FAST step, which cannot govern the rate.

That is the whole point of the question. The balanced equation \(\mathrm{A_2} + \mathrm{B_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{AB}\) suggests second order; the MECHANISM says first. Order is a property of the mechanism, not of the stoichiometry, which is why it must be measured rather than read off.

rows.stem: Decarboxylation of sodium benzoate on heating with soda lime gives :
rows.solution:
Decarboxylation of sodium benzoate gives BENZENE.

Heating the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid with soda lime — sodium hydroxide with calcium oxide — removes the carboxyl group as carbonate and leaves a hydrocarbon with ONE CARBON FEWER:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COONa} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NaOH}\ \text{and}\ \mathrm{CaO}} \mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\)

The hydrogen that replaces the carboxyl group goes onto the ring, so a seven-carbon salt gives a six-carbon hydrocarbon.

Toluene is the trap, and the carbon count is what excludes it: toluene has seven carbons, so getting it would mean the carboxyl group being REDUCED to a methyl group rather than removed. Calcium oxide is present not as a reagent but to keep the sodium hydroxide dry and manageable.

rows.subtopic: Nomenclature and Structure of Carbonyl Group
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — the substrate is printed as a two-dimensional condensed structural formula: a linear chain with each carbonyl oxygen set ABOVE its carbon and joined to it by a drawn double-bond mark. The LaTeX above reproduces that layout with \overset rather than approximating it, and every option is a text name, so the row is answerable from the stem alone. The compound is deliberately NOT named in words anywhere on this row because the question asks for its IUPAC name — naming it would state the answer. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The IUPAC name is 3-OXOBUTANAL.

Number from the end that gives the principal functional group the lower locant. Between an aldehyde and a ketone the ALDEHYDE has the higher priority, so it takes the suffix and becomes \(\mathrm{C_1}\).

Counting from there: \(\mathrm{C_1}\) is the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\), \(\mathrm{C_2}\) the \(-\mathrm{CH_2}-\), \(\mathrm{C_3}\) the ketone carbon, and \(\mathrm{C_4}\) the terminal methyl. Four carbons with the aldehyde as the suffix gives BUTANAL, and the ketone, being the junior group, is named as a PREFIX — oxo — at position 3.

The options test exactly this priority. Naming the compound as a "-one" would demote the aldehyde, which is not allowed; and "1-oxobutanal" would name the aldehyde carbon twice, once as the suffix and once as a prefix.

rows.stem: Dehydration of tertiary alcohols with Cu at 573 K gives :
rows.solution:
Dehydration of a TERTIARY alcohol over copper at 573 K gives an ALKENE.

Copper at this temperature dehydrogenates a primary alcohol to an aldehyde and a secondary alcohol to a ketone — in both cases by removing two hydrogens, one from the oxygen and one from the carbinol carbon.

A TERTIARY alcohol has NO hydrogen on its carbinol carbon, so that route is closed to it. What happens instead is DEHYDRATION: a molecule of water is lost, taking the hydroxyl and a hydrogen from a NEIGHBOURING carbon, and an alkene is formed.
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}OH} \xrightarrow[573\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{Cu}} (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{C{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

So the same catalyst at the same temperature gives three different products from the three classes of alcohol, and which one depends on what hydrogens are available.

rows.stem: Phenol on reaction with aqueous bromine at room temperature gives :
rows.solution:
Phenol with AQUEOUS BROMINE at room temperature gives 2,4,6-TRIBROMOPHENOL, as a white precipitate.

All three available positions are substituted at once, and no catalyst is needed. The hydroxyl group is strongly activating — its lone pair is fed into the ring, raising the electron density most at the ortho and para positions — and water helps further by letting the phenol ionise to phenoxide, which is more strongly activating still.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + 3\mathrm{Br_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_2Br_3OH} + 3\mathrm{HBr}\)

The MONObromo products are what a non-polar solvent gives: bromine in carbon disulphide at low temperature stops after one substitution and yields a mixture of the ortho and para isomers. The meta isomer is never a significant product, because the hydroxyl group does not activate that position.

rows.stem: The specific sequence in which amino acids are arranged in a protein is called :
rows.solution:
The sequence of amino acids is the PRIMARY STRUCTURE of a protein.

The four levels are distinguished by what they describe and what holds them together. The PRIMARY structure is the order of the residues along the chain, fixed by peptide bonds — and it is the level that determines all the others, since the folding follows from the sequence.

The SECONDARY structure is how the chain arranges itself locally, as an \(\alpha\)-helix or a \(\beta\)-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds between peptide linkages. The TERTIARY structure is the overall folding of the whole chain, and the QUATERNARY structure describes how several separate chains assemble, as the four subunits of haemoglobin do.

Denaturation destroys the secondary and tertiary structures while leaving the primary one intact — no peptide bond is broken.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) of \(\mathrm{O_2N - CH_2 - COOH}\) is lower than that of \(\mathrm{CH_3 - COOH}\).
Reason (R) : \(-\,\mathrm{NO_2}\) group shows electron withdrawing effect which increases the acidic character of \(\mathrm{O_2N - CH_2 - COOH}\).
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

A LOWER \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) means a STRONGER acid, and nitroethanoic acid is much the stronger of the two — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 1.7 against ethanoic acid's 4.76.

The Reason gives the cause exactly. The nitro group is strongly electron WITHDRAWING, both inductively and by resonance, so it pulls electron density along the chain. That pull helps disperse the negative charge on the carboxylate ion left behind after the proton departs, and a more stable anion means the proton leaves more readily.

Ethanoic acid has a METHYL group in the same position, which does the opposite — it releases electron density and concentrates the charge, making the acid weaker still.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Transition metals have high enthalpy of atomization.
Reason (R) : This is because transition metals have low melting points.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Transition metals do have high enthalpies of atomisation, because their \((n-1)d\) electrons take part in the metallic bonding alongside the \(ns\) electrons, and more electrons involved means stronger interatomic bonding.

But the Reason reverses the fact. Transition metals have HIGH melting points, not low ones — chromium melts at about 2130 K and tungsten at 3695 K. Zinc, cadmium and mercury are the exceptions, and precisely because their full d subshells contribute nothing to the bonding.

Corrected, the Reason would not have been an explanation anyway. Enthalpy of atomisation and melting point are both consequences of the strength of the metallic bonding — they run together, but neither causes the other.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : When NaCl is added in water, elevation in boiling point is observed.
Reason (R) : Elevation in boiling point is a colligative property.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Adding sodium chloride to water does elevate the boiling point, and elevation of boiling point is indeed a colligative property — both statements hold.

But the Reason CLASSIFIES the effect rather than explaining it. Saying that something is a colligative property tells us what KIND of property it is — one depending on the number of solute particles and not their nature — but not why adding a solute raises the boiling point at all.

The actual explanation is about vapour pressure. A non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the solvent, so the solution must be heated to a HIGHER temperature before its vapour pressure matches the atmospheric pressure and it boils.

A definition is not a cause, which is the distinction this question is testing.

rows.stem:
What happens when D-glucose is treated with the following reagents ?
(a) \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) water
(b) HCN
rows.solution:
(a) WITH BROMINE WATER, D-glucose is oxidised to a six carbon carboxylic acid, GLUCONIC ACID:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2}\text{ water}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)

Bromine water is a MILD oxidising agent — too mild to attack a hydroxyl group — so the only thing in the molecule it can have oxidised is the ALDEHYDE. That specificity is what makes the reaction a proof of the aldehyde group's presence.

Concentrated nitric acid is the contrast: being stronger, it oxidises BOTH ends and gives the dicarboxylic saccharic acid.

(b) WITH HYDROGEN CYANIDE, glucose forms a CYANOHYDRIN — the cyanide adds to the carbonyl carbon and the hydrogen to the oxygen:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{HCN} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH(OH)(CN)(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)

The product has SEVEN carbons where the sugar had six. That this nucleophilic addition works at all is one of the proofs that glucose contains a carbonyl group.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Write the chemical equations when :
(a) Pentan-3-one is treated with \(\mathrm{H_2N - NH_2}\) followed by heating with KOH in high boiling solvent such as ethylene glycol.
(b) Two molecules of \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C - CHO}\) are treated with conc. NaOH.
rows.solution:
(a) Hydrazine followed by a strong base in a high boiling solvent is WOLFF-KISHNER REDUCTION, which converts a carbonyl group all the way to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\). Hydrazine first condenses with the ketone to give the hydrazone, and heating that with the base expels nitrogen:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COCH_2CH_3} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{H_2N{-}NH_2}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2C({=}N{-}NH_2)CH_2CH_3} \xrightarrow[\text{ethylene glycol},\ \Delta]{\mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{N_2}\)

Pentan-3-one becomes n-pentane. The high boiling solvent is needed because the second stage requires a temperature well above what water would allow.

(b) 2,2-Dimethylpropanal has NO \(\alpha\)-hydrogen — the carbon next to its carbonyl is fully substituted by three methyl groups — so with concentrated alkali it cannot undergo aldol and undergoes the CANNIZZARO reaction instead. Two molecules react together, one being reduced and the other oxidised:
\(2(\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\mathrm{NaOH}} (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}CH_2OH} + (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}COO^-Na^+}\)

The products are 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol and sodium 2,2-dimethylpropanoate. It is a DISPROPORTIONATION — the same compound is both oxidised and reduced — and the absence of an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen is what makes it the only route available.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: Write two differences between order of reaction and molecularity of reaction.
rows.solution:
HOW EACH IS OBTAINED. ORDER is an EXPERIMENTAL quantity: it is found by measuring how the rate responds when concentrations are changed, and it cannot be read off the balanced equation. MOLECULARITY is THEORETICAL: it is the number of species that must collide in an elementary step, read off the proposed mechanism.

WHAT VALUES EACH CAN TAKE. ORDER may be zero, fractional or a whole number, since it is whatever the measurement gives. MOLECULARITY must be a WHOLE NUMBER and at least 1, since it counts colliding species and a fraction of a molecule cannot collide.

A third difference, if one is wanted: ORDER applies to elementary and complex reactions alike, whereas MOLECULARITY is defined only for an ELEMENTARY reaction — a complex reaction is a sequence of steps, each possibly with its own molecularity, so the sequence as a whole has none.

The two coincide only for an elementary reaction, where the single step IS the reaction.
